AWS RDS IAM Database Authentication¶

A step-by-step guide to replacing static Postgres passwords with AWS IAM database authentication, for deployments of SATHI on Amazon EC2 + Amazon RDS.

This guide is deployment-agnostic: every AWS-specific value is a placeholder (<...>) that you fill in from your own account. The steps were executed end-to-end on a live deployment (October 2026), and every pitfall documented here was hit and fixed on that deployment.

How it works¶

  • The app server’s EC2 instance profile (IAM role) lets the application mint a signed, 15-minute authentication token that is used in place of the password when connecting to RDS.

  • Token minting happens client-side (SigV4 signing inside the SDK): no AWS API call is made and nothing is recorded in CloudTrail. The IAM policy is evaluated by RDS when it validates the presented token.

  • A token only matters at connect time — established connections persist past token expiry. A fresh token is minted for every new connection, so long-lived web workers are fine at any CONN_MAX_AGE.

  • The RDS setting is a mode: “Password and IAM database authentication”. Enabling it never breaks existing password logins, which makes the migration staged and reversible.

  • A PostgreSQL user must be granted the ``rds_iam`` role to authenticate with tokens. A user with that role can use exactly one authentication method — the token, not a password.

Prerequisites¶

  • An RDS for PostgreSQL instance (9.6 or later; any current version works).

  • The application deployed on EC2 in the same VPC as the RDS instance (recommended; see the hardening phase).

  • AWS CLI v2 or AWS CloudShell, with a user holding IAM + RDS management rights, configured for the correct region.

  • The RDS master user password (needed once, in Phase 4).

  • psql is not preinstalled on a standard EC2 VM or in CloudShell. Install it where you need it:

    sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y postgresql-client

Phase 0 — Gather facts¶

From the AWS CLI (or CloudShell):

aws sts get-caller-identity
aws rds describe-db-instances \
  --query "DBInstances[].{id:DBInstanceIdentifier, resource:DbiResourceId, ver:EngineVersion, endpoint:Endpoint.Address, port:Endpoint.Port, public:PubliclyAccessible, vpcsg:VpcSecurityGroups}"

Collect:

  • ``DbiResourceId`` (db-XXXXXXXXXXXXX form) — required for the IAM policy ARN. The instance name (DBInstanceIdentifier) does not work in that ARN; using it is a very common cause of silent “access denied”.

  • Account ID, region, endpoint + port, engine version.

  • VPC ID, attached security group IDs, instance class.

  • The instance’s master database name versus the database the app uses — an RDS instance can host multiple databases.

  • The app server’s EC2 instance ID (on the VM: curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id).

  • PubliclyAccessible — if true, treat that as an incident-level finding and harden first (Phase 6).

  • Whether the instance is shared with other clients (other apps, DMS, other EC2 instances). Enabling IAM auth is inert to them, but later network changes are not — know who connects before you change anything.

Warning

If another workload shares the RDS instance, plan for it: it keeps working on password auth, but security-group and PubliclyAccessible changes affect it too.

Phase 1 — Create the IAM role and policy¶

Create the role (trust policy for EC2):

{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}

aws iam create-role --role-name <app>-app-role \
  --assume-role-policy-document file:///tmp/trust.json

Create a scoped policy. Note the ``DbiResourceId`` in the resource ARN:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "rds-db:Connect",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:rds-db:<region>:<account-id>:dbuser:db-<dbi-resource-id>/<app-db-user>"
  }]
}

aws iam create-policy --policy-name <app>-rds-iam-db-connect \
  --policy-document file:///tmp/rds-connect.json
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name <app>-app-role \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:policy/<app>-rds-iam-db-connect

The username in the ARN must match the database user name case-sensitively.

Warning

Do not add VPC condition keys to this policy. A tool may recommend adding "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:SourceVpc": "<vpc-id>"}} to restrict token use to one VPC. That is wrong: IAM database authentication does not support the global condition keys aws:SourceVpc, aws:SourceVpce, aws:SourceIp, aws:VpcSourceIp, aws:UserAgent or aws:Referer (see the RDS User Guide, “Limitations for IAM database authentication”). The rds-db service supports exactly one condition key: aws:ResourceTag/${TagKey}. An unsupported key is never present in the request context, so the condition never matches and every token-based connection is denied — the cutover breaks completely. The “only from this VPC” property is enforced at the network layer (private instance + security-group rules), not in the policy.

Phase 2 — Attach the role to the EC2 instance¶

A role cannot be attached to an instance directly — EC2 uses an instance profile (a container that holds the role):

aws iam create-instance-profile --instance-profile-name <app>-app-profile
aws iam add-role-to-instance-profile \
  --instance-profile-name <app>-app-profile \
  --role-name <app>-app-role
aws ec2 associate-iam-instance-profile \
  --instance-id i-<instance-id> \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=<app>-app-profile

Note

--iam-instance-profile Name= expects the profile name, not the role name. Passing the role name fails with InvalidParameterValue. The console flow masks this by auto-creating a profile named after the role — so “it worked from the console” does not mean the CLI form with the role name is valid.

Verify:

# from the AWS CLI:
aws ec2 describe-iam-instance-profile-associations \
  --filters Name=instance-id,Values=i-<instance-id>

# or from the VM (should report the role):
curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/info

The change is immediate; no reboot, and nothing running on the VM is affected until it next fetches credentials.

Phase 3 — Enable IAM authentication on the RDS instance¶

aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier <db-identifier> \
  --enable-iam-database-authentication --apply-immediately

The response is a snapshot at request time: it may still show IAMDatabaseAuthenticationEnabled: false with the change listed under PendingModifiedValues — that is normal. Re-verify within minutes:

aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier <db-identifier> \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].{iam: IAMDatabaseAuthenticationEnabled, pending: PendingModifiedValues}'

Expect iam: true and pending: {}. If it is still pending after ~10 minutes it has slipped to the maintenance window — investigate.

Also enable the ``iam-db-auth-error`` log export (console: Modify → Log exports). It is the troubleshooting trail for Phase 5.

Phase 4 — Create the database user and grants¶

From a machine with psql (the app VM, after the install from the prerequisites), connect as the master user:

PGPASSWORD='<master-password>' psql \
  "host=<endpoint> port=5432 dbname=<db-name> user=<master-user> sslmode=require"

Confirm who owns the existing tables (this drives the default-privilege FOR ROLE choice):

SELECT tablename, tableowner FROM pg_tables
WHERE schemaname='public' ORDER BY tablename LIMIT 10;

Create the user and grants (all as the master user):

CREATE USER <app-db-user>;              -- LOGIN by default, no password
GRANT rds_iam TO <app-db-user>;         -- REQUIRED for token auth

GRANT CONNECT, TEMP ON DATABASE <db-name> TO <app-db-user>;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO <app-db-user>;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO <app-db-user>;
GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public TO <app-db-user>;
-- sequence grants: auto-increment / bigserial primary keys need them

-- covers objects created *later* by the role that currently owns the
-- schema objects (<owner> — usually the master user):
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE <owner> IN SCHEMA public
  GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO <app-db-user>;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE <owner> IN SCHEMA public
  GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON SEQUENCES TO <app-db-user>;

Migrations need DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP), which the grants above do not include. Choose one:

  • A. ALTER SCHEMA public OWNER TO <app-db-user>; — the app user owns the schema and can migrate; broadest runtime rights.

  • B. A separate migration user with a password, used only by the deploy script — cleanest separation, one secret to manage.

  • C. GRANT CREATE ON SCHEMA public TO <app-db-user>; — the least-privilege option that fully suffices for migrate (new objects are self-owned). Recommended for a single-app deployment.

If the app user runs migrations, execute the chosen statement before the cutover, so a pending migration cannot fail at deploy time.

One role and one database user per connecting instance¶

If a second EC2 instance also connects to the same database, give it its own IAM role and its own least-privilege database user (its policy scoped to ...dbuser:db-<dbi-resource-id>/<second-db-user>). Rationale: least privilege (a compromised box inherits only its own grants), per-instance audit attribution, and independent lifecycle. Exception: if the second instance runs the same application (spare/replica web server), sharing one DB user — and thus one role — is acceptable. Migrating one app does not block the others: the instance stays in Password-and-IAM mode, so other clients keep working on passwords until their own cutover.

Phase 5 — Verify the token path before touching the app¶

On the app VM, mint a token using the instance role. With the AWS CLI:

TOKEN=$(aws rds generate-db-auth-token \
  --region <region> \
  --hostname <endpoint> \
  --port 5432 \
  --username <app-db-user>)

Without the AWS CLI (using the venv’s boto3, which the app package pulls in anyway):

cd /var/www/<app> && source venv/bin/activate
TOKEN=$(python -c "import boto3; print(boto3.session.Session().client('rds', region_name='<region>').generate_db_auth_token(DBHostname='<endpoint>', Port=5432, DBUsername='<app-db-user>'))")

Sanity-check, then connect:

echo ${#TOKEN}    # a real token is ~1800 chars; 0 means the var is empty

PGPASSWORD="$TOKEN" psql \
  "host=<endpoint> port=5432 dbname=<db-name> user=<app-db-user> sslmode=require" \
  -c 'SELECT current_user' -c '\dt'

Expect current_user to be the app user and the table list to be returned. That one success proves the whole chain: role → policy → token → rds_iam grant → table grants → security-group path → TLS.

If psql is unavailable, the app-level equivalent is python manage.py check --database default (it opens a real connection).

If it fails, check in this order:

  1. IAM policy ARN — db-… resource ID, username case, region, account.

  2. GRANT rds_iam TO <app-db-user>; present.

  3. Security-group path from the VM to the instance.

  4. The iam-db-auth-error CloudWatch log (Phase 3).

App-side changes¶

Requirements¶

django-iam-dbauth==0.2.1

Pin the version. The package wraps Django’s own PostgreSQL backend (works with psycopg2), mints a fresh token in get_connection_params() (per connection — safe with long-lived workers), and resolves CNAMEs so tokens are signed for the canonical endpoint (disable with resolve_cname_enabled: False for private endpoints or custom CNAMEs).

Note

There is no pip package for the RDS CA certificate bundle (the rds-ca-bundle name does not exist on PyPI), and certifi is the wrong bundle (Mozilla’s public CAs — Amazon’s RDS CA is not in it). Certificate verification uses a downloaded PEM; see the TLS section below.

Settings (open-source friendly)¶

The app also deploys in non-AWS environments, so IAM auth must be opt-in: a single flag switches the backend; without it the app behaves exactly as before. Nothing AWS-specific is loaded unless a deployment explicitly opts in:

DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': os.environ.get('DJANGO_DATABASE_ENGINE', 'django.db.backends.sqlite3'),
        'NAME': os.environ.get('DJANGO_DATABASE_NAME', 'db.sqlite3'),
        'USER': os.environ.get('DJANGO_DATABASE_USER', ''),
        'HOST': os.environ.get('DJANGO_DATABASE_HOST', 'localhost'),
        'PORT': os.environ.get('DJANGO_DATABASE_PORT', '5432'),
    }
}

if os.getenv('DJANGO_DATABASE_IAM_AUTH', 'False') == 'True':
    # Postgres-only path (RDS). The password is never read or sent.
    DATABASES['default'].update({
        'ENGINE': 'django_iam_dbauth.aws.postgresql',
        'PASSWORD': '',
        'OPTIONS': {
            'use_iam_auth': True,
            'sslmode': os.getenv('DJANGO_DATABASE_SSL_MODE', 'require'),
            # once the RDS CA bundle PEM is available on the host:
            # 'sslmode': 'verify-full',
            # 'sslrootcert': '/path/to/rds-global-bundle.pem',
        },
    })
else:
    DATABASES['default']['PASSWORD'] = os.environ.get('DJANGO_DATABASE_PASSWORD', '')

Properties of this design:

  • The flag is orthogonal to the environment variable that selects dev/staging/prod — every non-AWS deployment keeps working unchanged.

  • django_iam_dbauth is imported only when the engine is actually used, so non-AWS hosts never touch it (keeping it in requirements.txt makes deploys uniform).

  • sslmode is environment-driven, so the follow-up to verify-full is a .env change, not a code change.

Environment (.env)¶

AWS production host:

AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=<region>     # botocore reads *credentials* from the
                                # instance metadata but not the *region* —
                                # without it: NoRegionError on first connect
DJANGO_DATABASE_IAM_AUTH=True
DJANGO_DATABASE_ENGINE=django.db.backends.postgresql_psycopg2
DJANGO_DATABASE_NAME=<db-name>
DJANGO_DATABASE_USER=<app-db-user>
DJANGO_DATABASE_HOST=<endpoint>
DJANGO_DATABASE_PORT=5432
# DJANGO_DATABASE_PASSWORD is no longer needed

Any non-AWS production (unchanged from today): the flag stays unset and DJANGO_DATABASE_PASSWORD is provided as usual.

Warning

NoRegionError: You must specify a region on the first connection with the IAM backend means the host has no region configured anywhere botocore looks (no AWS_DEFAULT_REGION env var, no ~/.aws/config). botocore resolves credentials from instance metadata but not the region. Set AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=<region> in the app’s .env (load_dotenv puts it in the environment before any DB connection); the alternative is passing region_name in the OPTIONS dict.

TLS hardening (fast follow-up, after the cutover works)¶

sslmode=require (the default) encrypts but does not verify the server. To verify, download the RDS CA bundle from AWS’s PKI trust store (the global bundle covers all current RDS CAs and supersedes the legacy s3.amazonaws.com/rds-downloads/… URLs):

sudo mkdir -p /var/www/<app>/certs
sudo curl -o /var/www/<app>/certs/rds-global-bundle.pem \
  https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/global/global-bundle.pem

Then switch OPTIONS to sslmode: verify-full plus sslrootcert pointing at the PEM, and re-test the connection. Do not point sslrootcert at certifi — the RDS CA is not in it and verification will fail.

Deployment and cutover¶

Cutover order (why it is safe):

Phase 1–2  role + profile + attach   → inert
Phase 3    enable IAM auth           → inert (password logins unaffected)
Phase 4    user + grants             → inert
Phase 5    token test                → proves readiness without deploying
Deploy     app-side changes + restart → the actual cutover
Phase 6    hardening

Deploy (typical supervisor/gunicorn setup):

# update the server's .env as above, commit + push, then:
git pull
pip install -r requirements.txt
python manage.py migrate        # first live exercise of the new path —
                                # also proves the migration DDL grant
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
sudo supervisorctl restart all  # gunicorn and the celery worker

Verify after restart:

python manage.py check --database default   # must report no issues

Plus a quick look at the app itself, and watch CloudWatch IamDbAuthConnectionFailure and the iam-db-auth-error log for the first few minutes.

Rollback¶

If anything fails after the switch: redeploy the previous settings (commit) and restart — the password path still works, because the instance runs in Password and IAM mode. Full reversal, if ever needed:

aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier <db-identifier> \
  --no-enable-iam-database-authentication

-- as the master user; a token-only user has no password, so revoke
-- first, then set a password only if you want one:
REVOKE rds_iam FROM <app-db-user>;
-- ALTER USER <app-db-user> PASSWORD '...';

Phase 6 — Hardening and operations¶

  • Break-glass access: store the master password in AWS Secrets Manager (or a password manager) and document the Phase 5 token + psql commands so a human can reach the database in an incident.

  • Remove old credentials: drop the DJANGO_DATABASE_PASSWORD line from the server .env; rotate or delete any former application account. Check supervisor environment files — any process still reading a stale password will silently keep the old path.

  • Clock: confirm NTP (chrony/systemd-timesyncd) is active — signed tokens are clock-sensitive.

  • IMDS: confirm IMDSv2 (Require) on the instance; relevant if you ever containerise (IMDSv2 hop limit).

  • Monitoring: CloudWatch publishes IamDbAuthConnectionRequests / IamDbAuthConnectionSuccess / IamDbAuthConnectionFailure — alarm on any failure.

  • Snapshots: restores inherit the IAM-auth setting; no action needed.

  • Network posture: PubliclyAccessible should be false (for a VPC-resident instance that is a one-parameter modify-db-instance --no-publicly-accessible change), and 5432 reachable only from the app security groups — never 0.0.0.0/0 (leftover “for DMS migration”-style rules are a common finding and should be revoked). Remember the shared-instance caveat when changing anything network-level.

  • Future move to ECS/EKS: replace the instance profile with a task role / service account carrying the same policy.

Known limits and pitfalls¶

  • Token expiry (15 min) is a non-issue for established connections, but connection churn (e.g. CONN_MAX_AGE = 0 with many workers) multiplies token minting and IAM-auth connection attempts. Keep CONN_MAX_AGE sensible.

  • Connection-rate ceiling: RDS historically capped new IAM-auth connections at ~200/second; as of June 2026 the rate scales with instance resources. On the smallest instance classes expect the traditional low ceiling.

  • ``NoRegionError`` → set AWS_DEFAULT_REGION in the app .env (see the warning above).

  • ``aws:SourceVpc`` and friends are unsupported for rds-db — adding them breaks every connection (see the Phase 1 warning).

  • Instance profile ≠ role for associate-iam-instance-profile.

  • ``psql`` is not preinstalled anywhere by default.

  • ``sslmode=require`` encrypts without verifying; move to verify-full with the truststore PEM for the stronger posture.
